parts.problem_md:
The revenue (money received before expenses, tax, etc.) that Modx makes from selling maths t-shirts is found by multiplying the selling price by the number of items sold. Last year the company sold 8000 t-shirts at a price of £12 each, giving a revenue of £96 000.

This year, to maximise their revenue, Modx intend to increase the t-shirt price by £$x$. Each price increase of £1 is expected to reduce the number of items sold by 400.

The expected revenue for this year is modelled by

$R = 96  000 + 3200 x - 400 x^{2}$

where £$x$ is the increase in price per item.

By factorising $3200 x - 400 x^{2}$ and completing the square, show that the expected revenue can be written as `R = 102\,400 - 400\left(x - 4\right)^{2}`.
parts.solution_md:
Factorise the variable terms, taking out $- 400$

`3200x - 400x^{2} = -400\left(x^{2} - 8x\right)`

**[M1]**

Complete the square inside the bracket

`-400\left(x^{2} - 8x\right) = -400\left[\left(x - 4\right)^{2} - 16\right] = -400\left(x - 4\right)^{2} + 6400`

**[M1]**

Substitute back into the revenue model

`R = 96\,000 + 6400 - 400\left(x - 4\right)^{2}`

`R = 102\,400 - 400\left(x - 4\right)^{2}`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Factorises $3200 x - 400 x^{2}$ as `-400\left(x^{2} - 8x\right)`.
> 
> **M1**: Completes the square to reach `-400\left(x - 4\right)^{2} + 6400` or equivalent.
> 
> **A1**: Combines with 96 000 to obtain the given `R = 102\,400 - 400\left(x - 4\right)^{2}`.

parts.problem_md:
The number of toys, $P$, produced by a machine in one hour is modelled by

`P\left(T\right) = \left(20 - T\right)\left(T - 40\right) \qquad 20 \leq T \leq 40`

where the temperature of the machine is $T$ °C.

Find the number of toys produced in one hour when the temperature of the machine is 25 °C.
parts.solution_md:
Substitute $T = 25$ into the model

`P\left(25\right) = \left(20 - 25\right)\left(25 - 40\right) = \left(-5\right)\left(-15\right)`

$P = 75 \text{toys}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Substitutes $T = 25$ and evaluates to 75 toys.

parts.problem_md:
(i) Show that `P\left(T\right) = 60T - T^{2} - 800`.

(ii) By completing the square, show that `P\left(T\right) = 100 - \left(T - 30\right)^{2}`.

(iii) Hence find the temperature at which the machine is most productive, and the number of toys it produces in one hour at this temperature.
parts.solution_md:
(i)

Expand the brackets

`P\left(T\right) = 20T - 800 - T^{2} + 40T`

**[M1]**

`P\left(T\right) = 60T - T^{2} - 800`

**[A1]**

(ii)

Take out a factor of $- 1$ from the $T$ terms, then complete the square

`P\left(T\right) = -\left(T^{2} - 60T\right) - 800 = -\left[\left(T - 30\right)^{2} - 900\right] - 800`

**[M1]**

`P\left(T\right) = 100 - \left(T - 30\right)^{2}`

**[A1]**

(iii)

Since `\left(T - 30\right)^{2} \geq 0`, the value of $P$ is greatest when `\left(T - 30\right)^{2} = 0`

$T = 30 \text{°C}$

**[B1]**

$P = 100 \text{toys}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Expands `\left(20 - T\right)\left(T - 40\right)` with all four terms.
> 
> **A1**: Simplifies to the given `P\left(T\right) = 60T - T^{2} - 800`.
> 
> **M1**: Completes the square on `-\left(T^{2} - 60T\right)`, reaching `-\left[\left(T - 30\right)^{2} - 900\right]` or equivalent.
> 
> **A1**: Obtains the given `P\left(T\right) = 100 - \left(T - 30\right)^{2}`.
> 
> **B1**: Most productive temperature $T = 30$ °C (from the maximum of the completed square).
> 
> **B1**: Maximum number of toys is 100.

parts.problem_md:
A patient takes a new medication at midday. The amount of drug, $D$ mg, remaining in their bloodstream $h$ hours after midday is modelled by

`D\left(h\right) = 1 + 6h - h^{2} \qquad 0 \leq h \leq 6`

(i) Evaluate `D\left(0\right)` and hence state the amount of drug in the patient's bloodstream before they take any medication.

(ii) Find the amount of drug in the patient's bloodstream at 2 pm.

(iii) Show that by 6 pm the amount of drug in the patient's bloodstream has returned to its starting amount.
parts.solution_md:
(i)

Substitute $h = 0$ into the model

`D\left(0\right) = 1 + 6\left(0\right) - \left(0\right)^{2}`

`D\left(0\right) = 1 \text{ mg}`

**[B1]**

There is 1 mg of the drug already present in the bloodstream before any medication is taken

**[B1]**

(ii)

2 pm is 2 hours after midday, so $h = 2$

`D\left(2\right) = 1 + 6\left(2\right) - \left(2\right)^{2} = 1 + 12 - 4`

**[M1]**

`D\left(2\right) = 9 \text{ mg}`

**[A1]**

(iii)

6 pm is 6 hours after midday, so $h = 6$

`D\left(6\right) = 1 + 6\left(6\right) - \left(6\right)^{2} = 1 + 36 - 36`

**[M1]**

`D\left(6\right) = 1 \text{ mg}`

**Final answer:** **This equals **`D\left(0\right) = 1`** mg, so the amount has returned to its starting value**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Evaluates `D\left(0\right) = 1`.
> 
> **B1**: States that 1 mg is present before the medication is taken.
> 
> **M1**: Substitutes $h = 2$ into the model.
> 
> **A1**: Correct amount of 9 mg.
> 
> **M1**: Substitutes $h = 6$ into the model.
> 
> **A1**: Obtains 1 mg and states this equals the starting amount `D\left(0\right)`.

parts.problem_md:
The revenue a company makes from selling an item is the selling price multiplied by the number of items sold. Last year Toys-were-Us sold 3 million computer games at a price of £50 each.

This year Toys-were-Us wish to maximise their revenue, but a change in price will change the number of games sold: for every £2 increase in price, sales fall by 500 000; and for every £2 decrease in price, sales rise by 500 000.

Find the price at which Toys-were-Us should sell computer games this year in order to maximise revenue, and state the expected number of games sold and the expected revenue.
parts.solution_md:
Let $x$ be the number of £2 increases in the price (so $x$ is negative for a price decrease). Then the selling price is `\left(50 + 2x\right)` and the number of games sold is `\left(3 - \tfrac{1}{2}x\right)` million

$\text{price} = 50 + 2 x ,  \text{number} = 3 - \frac{1}{2} x \text{(millions)}$

**[M1]**

Revenue, in £ millions

`R = \left(50 + 2x\right)\left(3 - \tfrac{1}{2}x\right) = 150 - 19x - x^{2}`

**[M1]**

Complete the square

`R = -\left[\left(x + 9.5\right)^{2} - 90.25\right] + 150 = 240.25 - \left(x + 9.5\right)^{2}`

**[M1]**

The revenue is greatest when $x = - 9 . 5$

$x = - 9 . 5$

**[A1]**

`\text{price} = 50 + 2\left(-9.5\right) = \text{£}31`

$\text{price} = \text{£} 31$

**[A1]**

`\text{number} = 3 - \tfrac{1}{2}\left(-9.5\right) = 7.75 \text{ million}`

$7 . 75 \text{million games} ,  \text{revenue} = \text{£} 240 . 25 \text{million}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Writes the price as `\left(50 + 2x\right)` and the number sold as `\left(3 - \tfrac{1}{2}x\right)` million (allowing $x$ to be negative).
> 
> **M1**: Forms the revenue product and expands to $150 - 19 x - x^{2}$.
> 
> **M1**: Completes the square.
> 
> **A1**: Maximum at $x = - 9 . 5$ (from the completed square, not calculus).
> 
> **A1**: Selling price of £31.
> 
> **A1**: 7.75 million games and revenue £240.25 million.

where $h$ m is the height of the skydiver above the ground and $x$ m is the horizontal distance along the ground from $O$.

parts.problem_md:
The leakage rate of water from a pipe, $L$ litres per second, is directly proportional to the square root of the flow rate $s$ m s⁻¹, which is the speed of the water flowing through the pipe. It is observed that the leakage rate is 0.72 litres per second when the flow rate is 0.64 m s⁻¹.

Write down an equation connecting $L$ and $s$.
parts.solution_md:
Proportional to the square root of the flow rate

$L = k \sqrt{s}   \Rightarrow   0 . 72 = k \sqrt{0.64} = 0 . 8 k   \Rightarrow   k = 0 . 9$

**[M1]**

$L = 0 . 9 \sqrt{s}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Writes $L = k \sqrt{s}$ and substitutes the given values to find $k$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation $L = 0 . 9 \sqrt{s}$.

parts.problem_md: Find the flow rate when the leakage rate is 0.49 litres per second.
parts.solution_md:
Substitute $L = 0 . 49$

$0 . 49 = 0 . 9 \sqrt{s}   \Rightarrow   \sqrt{s} = \frac{0.49}{0.9}$

**[M1]**

$s = 0 . 296 \text{m s}^{-1}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Substitutes $L = 0 . 49$ and rearranges for $\sqrt{s}$.
> 
> **A1**: $s = 0 . 296$ m s⁻¹ (answers which round to 0.296).

parts.problem_md: An alternative model for the leakage rate is $L = 0 . 5 s$. Other than when there is no leak, find a flow rate and a leakage rate for which both models predict the same result.
parts.solution_md:
Both models are equal when $0 . 9 \sqrt{s} = 0 . 5 s$

$0 . 9 \sqrt{s} = 0 . 5 s   \Rightarrow   0 . 9 = 0 . 5 \sqrt{s}   \Rightarrow   \sqrt{s} = 1 . 8$

**[M1]**

`s = 3.24 \text{ m s}^{-1}, \quad L = 0.5\left(3.24\right) = 1.62 \text{ litres per second}`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Sets the two models equal and solves for the non-zero flow rate ($\sqrt{s} = 1 . 8$, so $s = 3 . 24$).
> 
> **A1**: Flow rate 3.24 m s⁻¹ and leakage rate 1.62 litres per second.

parts.problem_md:
A fountain is designed so that water is projected over a walkway. The path of the water is modelled by

`y = x\left(5 - x\right) , 0 \leq x \leq 5`

where $x$ is the horizontal distance in metres from the base of the fountain at ground level and $y$ is the height of the water in metres.

Sketch the graph of the model, labelling any intersections with the coordinate axes.
parts.solution_md:
The model `y = x\left(5 - x\right)` is a negative quadratic (an $\cap$-shaped parabola) that meets the $x$-axis where $y = 0$

`x\left(5 - x\right) = 0 \Rightarrow x = 0 \text{ or } x = 5`

The curve meets the $x$-axis at `\left(0, 0\right)` and `\left(5, 0\right)`, with its maximum on the line of symmetry $x = 2 . 5$, at `\left(2.5, 6.25\right)`

![Sketch of the inverted parabola y = x(5 - x) for 0 to 5, meeting the x-axis at (0, 0) and (5, 0) with maximum at (2.5, 6.25)](assets/003-sketch-of-the-inverted-parabola-y-x-5-x-for-0-to.png)

**[B1 B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct $\cap$-shaped parabola for $0 \leq x \leq 5$, not extending below the $x$-axis.
> 
> **B1**: Both $x$-axis intersections labelled, `\left(0, 0\right)` and `\left(5, 0\right)`.

parts.problem_md:
The average person is 1.7 m tall and needs a ground width of 1.2 m in order to walk comfortably.

Work out the maximum number of average-sized people who can comfortably walk under the fountain side by side without getting wet.
parts.solution_md:
A person stays dry where the water is at least 1.7 m high, so find the $x$-values where $y = 1 . 7$

`x\left(5 - x\right) = 1.7 \Rightarrow x^{2} - 5x + 1.7 = 0`

$x = \frac{5\pm\sqrt{25-6.8}}{2} = 0 . 36697 \dots \text{or} 4 . 63303 \dots$

**[M1]**

The width of the gap in which a person can stand upright and stay dry is the distance between these values

$\text{width} = 4 . 63303 \dots - 0 . 36697 \dots = 4 . 2661 \text{m}$

**[A1]**

Each person needs 1.2 m, so divide and round down (a fourth person would need $4 \times 1 . 2 = 4 . 8$ m, which does not fit)

$\frac{4.2661}{1.2} = 3 . 55 \dots$

$3 \text{people}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Sets $y = 1 . 7$ and solves $x^{2} - 5 x + 1 . 7 = 0$ for the two $x$-values.
> 
> **A1**: Correct usable width — answers which round to 4.27 m (using unrounded roots $4 . 633 - 0 . 367$).
> 
> **A1**: 3 people. Accept 3 only — the count is rounded down, since a fourth person would not fit.

parts.problem_md:
The Blue Blades Aerobatic Display Team use white and blue smoke trails in their flying display. At the start of the display, each aeroplane holds a tank containing 360 litres of white smoke fluid and a separate tank of blue smoke fluid.

The amount of white smoke fluid remaining, $w$ litres, after $t$ seconds of use is modelled by

$w = \frac{k}{t+p} - q$

where $k$, $p$ and $q$ are positive constants.

(i) Given that $q = 90$ and that it takes 50 seconds for the amount of white smoke fluid to halve, find the values of $k$ and $p$.

(ii) Hence find the number of minutes of use that a tank of 360 litres of white smoke fluid will last.
parts.solution_md:
(i) At the start, $t = 0$ and the tank is full, $w = 360$

$360=\frac{k}{p}-90\Rightarrow\frac{k}{p}=450\Rightarrowk=450p$

**[M1]**

After 50 s the fluid has halved, $w = 180$

$180 = \frac{k}{50+p} - 90   \Rightarrow   \frac{k}{50+p} = 270$

**[M1]**

Substitute $k = 450 p$

`450p = 270\left(50 + p\right) \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; 180p = 13\,500`

parts.problem_md: The average person is 1.7 m tall and needs a ground width of 1.2 m in order to walk comfortably. Find the distance at ground level between the two points where the water height is 1.7 m.
parts.solution_md:
Set the height equal to 1.7

`x\left(4 - x\right) = 1.7 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; x^{2} - 4x + 1.7 = 0`

$x = \frac{4\pm\sqrt{9.2}}{2} = 0 . 4835 \dots   \text{or}   3 . 5164 \dots$

**[M1]**

$\text{width} = 3 . 5164 \dots - 0 . 4835 \dots = 3 . 03 \text{m}$

> **A1**: Distance between the roots = 3.03 m (answers which round to 3.03).

parts.problem_md:
The leakage rate of water from a pipe, $L$ litres per second, is directly proportional to the flow rate $s$ m s⁻¹, which is the speed of the water flowing through the pipe. It is observed that the leakage rate is 0.3 litres per second when the flow rate is 0.6 m s⁻¹.

Show that the constant of proportionality is 0.5, and hence write down an equation connecting $L$ and $s$.
parts.solution_md:
The leakage rate is directly proportional to the flow rate

$L = k s$

Substitute $L = 0 . 3$ and $s = 0 . 6$

$0 . 3 = k \times 0 . 6$

$k = 0 . 5   \Rightarrow   L = 0 . 5 s$

parts.problem_md:
The White Blades Aerobatic Display Team use white smoke trails in their flying display. At the start of the display, each aeroplane holds a tank containing 180 litres of white smoke fluid. The amount of white smoke fluid, $W$ litres, remaining in a tank is inversely proportional to the total time, $t$ seconds, for which white smoke has been produced, plus 25 seconds.

Find an equation modelling the relationship between $W$ and $t$.
parts.solution_md:
Inverse proportion to `\left(t + 25\right)` gives

$W = \frac{k}{t+25}$

**[M1]**

At the start, $t = 0$ and the tank is full, so $W = 180$

$180 = \frac{k}{25}   \Rightarrow   k = 4500$

**[M1]**

$W = \frac{4500}{t+25}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Writes the inverse proportion as $W = \frac{k}{t+25}$.
> 
> **M1**: Uses $t = 0$, $W = 180$ to find $k = 4500$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct model $W = \frac{4500}{t+25}$.

parts.problem_md: The smoke-producing mechanism becomes unreliable once the amount of white smoke fluid remaining drops below 7% of the initial amount. Find the maximum whole number of minutes for which each aeroplane can reliably produce white smoke.
parts.solution_md:
7% of the initial 180 litres

$0 . 07 \times 180 = 12 . 6 \text{litres}$

**[M1]**

Solve $W = 12 . 6$

$\frac{4500}{t+25} = 12 . 6   \Rightarrow   t + 25 = 357 . 1 \dots   \Rightarrow   t = 332 \text{s} = 5 . 5 \dots \text{min}$

**[M1]**

$\text{maximum reliable time} = 5 \text{minutes}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Finds the critical amount $0 . 07 \times 180 = 12 . 6$ litres.
> 
> **M1**: Solves $\frac{4500}{t+25} = 12 . 6$ for $t$ (accept in seconds, ≈ 332 s).
> 
> **A1**: Rounds **down** to 5 whole minutes (6 minutes would already be unreliable).

parts.solution_md:

**[B1]**

parts.problem_md:
A machine produces toys at a rate that depends on the machine's temperature; the more extreme the temperature, the less productive it is. The productivity is modelled by

`P\left(T\right) = 0.02T\left(5 - T\right)\left(T - 60\right), \quad 5 \leq T \leq 60`

where $P$ is the number of toys produced per hour and the temperature of the machine is $T$ °C.

Find the number of toys produced per hour when the temperature of the machine is 36 °C.
parts.solution_md:
`P\left(36\right) = 0.02\left(36\right)\left(5 - 36\right)\left(36 - 60\right) = 535.68`

**[M1]**

The model gives a rate of 535.68, so the machine makes 535 or 536 whole toys per hour

$P = 536 \text{toys}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Substitutes $T = 36$ into the model and evaluates to 535.68.
> 
> **A1**: States a single whole number — accept 535 or 536. Must be a positive integer; do not accept the decimal 535.68 or an approximation symbol.

parts.problem_md: Show that `P\left(T\right) = 1.3T^{2} - 0.02T^{3} - 6T`.
parts.solution_md:
Expand the two brackets first

`\left(5 - T\right)\left(T - 60\right) = -T^{2} + 65T - 300`

`P\left(T\right) = 0.02T\left(-T^{2} + 65T - 300\right)`

**[M1]**

`P\left(T\right) = 1.3T^{2} - 0.02T^{3} - 6T`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Expands `\left(5 - T\right)\left(T - 60\right)` correctly and multiplies by $0 . 02 T$.
> 
> **A1**: Obtains the given `P\left(T\right) = 1.3T^{2} - 0.02T^{3} - 6T` with no errors.

parts.solution_md:
`P\left(41\right) = 0.02\left(41\right)\left(5 - 41\right)\left(41 - 60\right) = 560.88`

**[M1]**

The model gives a rate of 560.88, so the machine makes 560 or 561 whole toys per hour

$P = 561 \text{toys}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Substitutes $T = 41$ into the model and evaluates to 560.88.
> 
> **A1**: States a single whole number — accept 560 or 561. Must be a positive integer; do not accept the decimal 560.88 or an approximation symbol.

parts.problem_md: Suggest a reason why the machine cannot operate below 5 °C.
parts.solution_md:

parts.problem_md:
It has often been said that, to avoid relegation from football's Premier League, a team should aim to score at least 40 points in a season. Each team plays 38 games; a win is rewarded with 3 points and a draw with 1 point. No points are awarded for a loss.

Using $W$ and $D$ as the number of wins and draws respectively, write down an inequality describing the number of points a team should aim for to avoid relegation.
parts.solution_md:
A win gives 3 points and a draw gives 1 point, so the total is $3 W + D$, which must be at least 40

$3 W + D \geq 40$

**[B1 B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct points expression $3 W + D$.
> 
> **B1**: Correct inequality $3 W + D \geq 40$ (accept $\geq$; a strict $>$ is not accepted, since exactly 40 avoids relegation).

parts.problem_md:
Another condition on $W$ and $D$ is $W + D \leq 38$.

(i) Briefly explain why this second condition arises.

(ii) Explain why $W \geq 0$ and $D \geq 0$ must also be conditions.
parts.solution_md:
(i)

**Final answer:** **The number of wins and draws added together cannot be more than the 38 games played in a season**

**[B1]**

(ii)

**Final answer:** **The number of wins and the number of draws are each a count of games, so neither can be negative**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Explains that $W + D$ counts games that are not losses, and only 38 games are played.
> 
> **B1**: Explains that $W$ and $D$ are counts (numbers of games), so cannot be negative.

parts.problem_md: A team has won 3 games and drawn 5 after playing 19 games. Write down an updated inequality for the number of points required during the remainder of the season in order to avoid relegation.
parts.solution_md:
Points already gained from 3 wins and 5 draws

`3\left(3\right) + 5 = 14 \text{ points}`

A further $40 - 14 = 26$ points are needed from the remaining games

**[M1]**

$3 W + D \geq 26$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Finds the points already gained ($14$) and subtracts from 40 (or equivalent complete method).
> 
> **A1**: Correct updated inequality $3 W + D \geq 26$ (with $W$, $D$ now counting the remaining games).
